CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: LEWIS (West Huron) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 60) to amend the Criminal Code respecting injuries to persons due to motor vehicles.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-INJURIES DUE TO MOTOR VEHICLES.
speechtext:
This Bill proposes to deal with a class of offences upon our highways caused by vehicles that were not in common use at the time the Criminal Code was introduced, I refer to automobiles. While I understand that this parliament has no control over the King's highway,

still persons in the rural districts who built the highways for their own use are now very much troubled by automobiles. This Bill proposes to punish drivers of automobiles who are reckless, and who violate the law. It is modelled on the Bill introduced last session in reference to the same matter. I trust that the government, if they do not see fit to allow this Bill to pass, will at least add an amendment to the Criminal Code providing the needed legislation and place on crown officials the duty of finding and prosecuting drivers who break the law. It is true that the owner of an automobile has to keep his vehicle numbered, but when you are tangled up in the ditch with a frightened horse, there is little time given to find the number. I have here an item from the Toronto ' Mail and Empire.' which says that automobiles coming round the corners and dashing through crowds are becoming a menace to people travelling on the streets of Toronto.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: House again in committee to consider the proposed resolution granting an increase of salaries to civil servants.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This resolution has been before the committee for some time, and I do not know whether any further discussion is required. A Bill will be introduced founded upon it, but in the meantime I will be glad to answer any questions.

I made an objection to a certain part of this resolution the other day, and asked the minister to look into it:
That all sums of money voted by parliament for the financial year ending on March 31, 1909, and applicable to the payment of salaries or increase of salaries of persons in the inside service shall be applicable to the payment of increases of salary granted under the Act to be founded in this resolution, so far as such sums are not required for the specific purposes for which they were granted; and during the said financial year there may be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such moneys required for the payment of increases of salary hereunder as have not been voted by parliament.
I did not see why it was necessary to have that now when parliament was assembled and it would be quite possible to name the exact amount which is necessary, to bring down an estimate and vote it in the regular way. I pointed out that it is an al-[DOT] together irregular way of arranging for expenditures-to take the whole consolidated revenue and dip into it as is necessary. The whole basis of parliamentary appropriation is a specific request for a specific purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The question is one of convenience in the payments. I do not think there would be any difference at all in the amount which would have to be paid out. This statute, when passed, will define clearly and distinctly what moneys have to be paid out. It would be a mere question of going over the lists of the Civil Service and calculating how much each one would receive and what the aggregate amount would be. It is hoped that this Bill will pass before long and that the payments will then be available for the civil servants. If the procedure of my hon. friend were adopted we would have to have a supplementary item in the estimates, a special item, probaly, put through for that purpose. I would not have any objection to it if there was any particular object to be gained, but I have not seen any object in it. The statute will define what the amount will be in conjunction with the lists which have been presented and which are before the House of all those who are eligible for this increase. I have had statements made up, copies of which I will lay on the table if desired, showing the exact amounts payable to practically every civil servant. Of course my hon. friend might say that with these copies we might at once make up an estimate. But if the Bill passes the money can then be paid over to the Civil Service without any further delay or waiting for a supplementary estimate to be passed. That is the only view I have in regard to the matter. I am not quarrelling at all with my hon. friend's suggestion, but we think that this is the better and the simpler way and the way that would most promptly give that relief to the Civil Service which is the object of the Bill.
Of course, what my hon. friend says, if it has any force in this case, would apply with equal force to every appropriation that is made for every part of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.
I think so. He says it will be more convenient because you would not have to come to parliament and ask for it. He says at the same time that he has exactly the amounts that are necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As far as I know.

If the minister has the amounts that are necessary, or, if he has not them and can get them, certainly the basis of parliamentary appropriation is plainly contravened if he receives a general power to take out of the consolidated fund the gross amount that is necessary What I think is objectionable is that there should be any break from what is the acknowledged system and basis unless there is necessity for it. There was a necessity last year because you could not tell what

the increases were. We asked in parliament what amount this would be and the answer was :	You cannot tell. Then,
parliament was proroguing and unless such a convenience as that were allowed at that time you would have to wait for another session of parliament. That was a good reason for it, but if parliament has been going right on last year we would not have submitted to that mode of procedure ; we would have asked the government to bring down specific amounts and have them voted. I do hope that the minister will not allow the plea of convenience to influence him in asking the House to depart from what has heretofore been the b3sis of parliamentary appropriation. He is doing it while parliament is in session and in a position to vote whatever is required.

If it is only a matter of convenience why do you not make your statute extend to the whole Civil Service instead of asking us to vote money from year to year to pay their salaries ? It would be more convenient to vote it by statute and not discuss it at all. But, that is not the wisdom of parliament; the wisdom of parliament is to have the money voted from year to year. While we annually vote a portion of the salaries another portion is paid by authority of statute. I do not think it a good principal. I think it is a very bad one. We do pay the judge's salaries by statute, but that is a different thing entirely. Judges are appointed for life and they get a certain specific sum, but we have never allowed the same principle to prevail in relation to votes by parliament for the Civil Service as. far as I know. It is a departure from what has been the established custom and I think the minister is not justified in asking the House to assent to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I appreciate fully the difference between this Bill and the Bill of last session and I also appreciate what the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said, that we ought not to depart from the usual practice of voting specific sums for a specific purpose unless there is very good reason for it. 1 am not set by any means against the proposition of my hon. friend. I only wish to discuss it a little and see whether we can work it out properly and satisfactorily. Would my hon. friend consider that we would have to specify all these several items or only take one lump sum to serve the purpose for the whole Civil Service ? I suppose, to follow the general practice, we would have to state that so much was needed for the Department of Agriculture, so much for the Department of Customs and so on. If that line is adopted I think it would be quite unnecessary to go into the details of each individual salary although in our ordinary civil government estimates we come very Mr. FOSTER.
close to that. It hardly seems to me that it will be at all necessary. The general principle of the addition to the pay of the service is laid down definitely and clearly in the statute and it cannot be departed from. The only question that arises is whe-there there will be 25, or 50 or 100 men who shall get $150, whether there will be 200 or 300 who shall get $100, whether so many others shall get $50 and so on. _ I would like, before coming to a conclusion, to go into that a little and see whither it is going to land us. At the same time I recognize the justice and force of what_ the hon. gentleman says with regard to this Bill as being different from the situation of the last Bill.

I think the minister sees the whole difficulty. If you make it a mere matter of the Act and allow the minister to go into the consolidated revenue fund you put it outside of all criticism by parliament. It is true that we adopt the principle of giving a flat increase, but that does not mean that the House is, therefore, giving up all its right to criticise where the money goes or to object _ if in a certain particular instance it thinks the whole $150 should not go to a certain individual. There is a scale under which some will get $150, there are other cases in which $150 will not be got, and in some cases no increase will be got. This is a matter that the House ought to have under its own purview and should be able to criticise. A statement should be submitted to the House for each department showing what the department is getting under this resolution. While nine-tenths of the cases will not call for any criticism, there are instances-I could name some-where we might wish to suggest that a less amount than $150 should be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not wish to cavil at what my hon. friend has said, generally it is quite correct; but if this statute is passed the estimate based upon it would be very much of the nature of a statutory estimate and the House could hardly refuse it. Of course, the Bill says that payments may be made on the report of the deputy minister, and it may be that some individuals are of such a character that the deputy minister would not feel justified in recommending this increase. The only way of carrying out my hon. friend's suggestion would be to have an estimate based on the reports of the deputy minister, and if the deputy minister had reported that so and so was entitled to this increase, I do not think that under the statute he could well refuse it.

I should be sorry to have to vote a lump sum and then have it said that it shall be expended on the judgment * of the deputy minister without any chance

for a member of parliament to criticise that judgment. In discussing the Bill I will be prepared to mention some cases in which the payments should not be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It has been suggested to me that a schedule might be attached to the Bill setting out the payments.
If that were done we would have a chance to criticise the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Then we will leave that open and discuss it later. I suppose a schedule giving the amounts for each department or each branch of a department would be quite sufficient P
Mr. FOSTER, That would be acceptable. When we come to discuss it, the question would be, how did the minister arrive at the schedule? The minister would explain and his judgment would be a matter of criticism.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It would practically be the same as an item in the estimates.

With that understanding, I for my part will let the resolution pass, but it is not to be understood that I agree with the resolution itself; for convenience and in order to get the Bill before the House I shall make my critisicms when the Bill itself is up.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If we chop out this part of the resolution we may have to insert something else, for we would have to have another resolution. We would be glad to make as much progress with the resolution as possible, and if any hon. gentlemen wish to bring up points that would require investigation before answering them, it would be an advantage to have them do so now.

I have been more busy gathering information than by digesting it. I have not all the information from all the departments yet. I find this a very complex and knotty question, and I do not know whether we will ever get at the bottom or basis of it. When the resolution is finally passed there will be a basis from which to start; but it is a terror, as the boys say, to get at it in all its bearings. The returns from the minister's own department are explicit. I will pay my hon. friend the compliment of saying that when his clerks send down a return, one can see what it means; but I cannot say that for some of the others, because if there is any way on God's earth for them to make it difficult to find out what they mean, some of these departments know how to do it and do it most religiously.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have tried to make mine plain.

For instance, my hon. friend had a very large number of persons in what is sometimes called the outside inside service and he loyally, I think, to the principle of the new Civil Service Act, transferred these men into the inside service at the ,salaries they were then enjoying. He did not go to the outside list and make preferences and give to scores or hundreds iof them increases of salary just prior to their being transferred into the permanent service. I do not want to say any thing harsh, but the assumption was that the men in the outside service were getting what the government thought was a fair provision for their needs-if they did not get that it was the fault of the minister-but, it does not seem to be carrying out the spirit of the Act that just prior to the fateful September 1, one or more ministers should take the officers of the outside service, give some of them $500 or $600 or $700 increase on their salaries and then throw them in a great heap into the new permanent service. I think that proceeding ought to have been carefully considered, and I think that what has been done by some, at least, of the ministers is open to criticism. Most of the departments took the spirit of the Act in the proper sense and brought in the officers of the outside service at the salaries they enjoyed up to that time, and therefore they did not raise salaries in special instances by amounts more or less large so as to put these particular officers on a footing which they otherwise would not have had. I do not think any government can afford to have a sense of injustice spring up amongst its employees. The Prime Minister is the guardian of his different departments and I do not think he can make it conform with his- sense ,of justice that one department should do for its outside employees that which another department does not do. In this case one department has adhered religiously to the spirit of the Act and the discussion in parliament and it has brought in the outside civil servants at the salaries they previously had, but another department puts 200 or 300 of its outside men on a more favoured basis just prior to the 1st of September and brings them into the permanent service. Two injustices are done by that. In the permanent service there were men who for years had performed their duty well; they received none of these increases and they therefore were placed at a disadvantage in having the outside men drafted into the inside service and placed over them. They do feel that is an injustice which ought not to have been perpetrated. Then there is an injustice as between the outside servants themselves. For instance, in the department of the Minister of Agriculture he thinks he ought not to increase the salaries of his outside servants before they come into the permanent service

bo that they might have higher salaries on the permanent basis. The outside men in that department are discriminated against in favour of the outside men in other departments in which a different course was followed. As I say, a double injutsice is perpetrated. On the face of it it looks like an injustice and no doubt the ministers who have taken this course will give their reasons for it. Then another thing was done. Just prior to the 1st of September new men were appointed to the outside service without any reference to the conditions of the Civil Service Act. They were appointed a few days prior to the 1st of September and then they stepped right in to the permanent service at the salaries allotted to them a few days previously. That does not seem to be fair. To the minister who .'thought there was absolute necessity for the appointment of these men three days before the 1st of September, it may be said that the service would not have been hurt if he had waited for three days longer and had these men appointed in accordance with the spirit of the new Civil Service Act. I am sorry to say there are a great many of these examples and it does not seem to me that they can be justified on the principle of equal justice to all. There is another point, and I present it more especially to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. He is in a sense an employer of labour ; on one side of the street he has a number of men working for him, and on the other side of the street he has in his employment a number of equally good men. The men on both sides of the street are doing the same kind of work for him, they are living under the same conditions, the increased cost of living bears as hardly on one class as on the other, and as an employer of labour how does the First Minister justify himself in raising the salaries of the men on one side of the street and in leaving the men on the other side without any consideration? My right hon. friend increases the salaries of men in the inside service but the men in tlie outside service who are working for him and under the same conditions get no alleviation of their condition. If it is worth while to do a thing at all it is worth while to do it right. This government has money enough, and had money enough, to enable the men in the outside service to cope with the more stringent conditions that have arisen on account of the increased cost of living, and the government should have treated all its employees alike and done even justice to all. There is a sense of injustice which must rankle in the breast of every man who sees his fellow provided for and who finds himself overlooked in that way. These are things that must be taken into .account, and when the proper time comes I shall cite individual instances to show what was done. Then, in the case of Mr. FOSTER.
these outside men whose salaries were raised and dated back in some cases for months and months involving a largely increased expenditure, I would like to know out of what fund this was done. Surely we cannot raise a man's salary unless we have an appropriation therefor, and I have been unable to discover where these appropriations existed. This seems to have been done by order in council and whether in the case of the outside men it goes before the Treasury Board or not I do not know. But at all events there seems substantial ground for criticism and I shall criticise that in detail at a later stage of the Bill. These are some of the points of criticism that I would like to bring to the attention of my hon. friends in general. We can go into them in detail later.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has taken this opportunity of saying what he has said, and I thank him for the compliments to myself.
Compliments to your clerks.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have tried to do what he suggests although there are but few cases in which I have been doing that which he has indicated. Let me explain one or two which may be taken as samples of the others. I have had for a good many years, cerealists at the experimental farm who are scientific men. There is Dr. Charles Saunders, who has qualifications very rare in Canada, and who was appointed on that account. My officers at the experimental farm, under Dr. Saunders, were, I thought, of a character which entitled them to the place in subdivision B of the first division, in which the minimum salary is $2,100. Dr. Charles SaundeTs, who was in receipt of a lower salary, should go, I thought, under the reorganization, into that subdivision at $2,100. Consequently I raised his salary by order in council shortly before the change, and I raised it for that express purpose, to $2,100. If I had not done so, I would have been hampered by the provisions of the Civil Service Act, because they would apply to a gentleman, who, before this Act came into force, was not in the inside service, and therefore had not the laws, regulations, and restrictions of the inside service applied to him. Before the 1st September last I could, by an order in council with my colleague's consent, raise Dr. Saunders' salary in any way I liked without being hampered by any statute. His salary was paid out of the lump vote for the experimental farm, as were all the salaries there, from Dr. Saunders down. My hon. friend asked where the money was got. That is one of a great many instances in which the salaries were paid out of lump votes, and if those lump votes were sufficient in the year to pay an increase, the increase could be given by order in council, or in some cases, by

ministerial order. A good many in the outside service were appointed by ministers, and their salaries could be and were raised at different times by minister's order. This particular instance is one of a kind which has occurred in other cases and which I am prepared to justify as perfectly fair and just. I have no doubt whatever that many ministers, having had the control and the power to raise the salaries in the outside service in Ottawa, took a good deal of pains and trouble, since the coming into force of the Act of last session to go into the adequacy and relative amounts of the salaries of the men who are paid out of these lump votes, knowing that after the first of September last they could not raise the salaries which were paid out of these votes, and which they thought they were justified in raising, without increasing others, because the new Act applied the rules and regulations of the Civil Service Act to those who before the first of last September did not come under those restrictions as to their salaries or appointments.
No doubt whatever a good many instan ces of that kind occurred. I have not examined the reorganization sufficiently in detail to know what my colleagues have been doing, but I know that in my own department there were some instances in which I did that.
My hon. friend has spoken of another class of employees, a class, he says, of employees who are working across the street but not in the same offices, and who did not get the benefit of these increases. That is quite right. There has also been brought to our attention the case of other men in other cities who say that they are in the public service just as much as the civil servants, so called, who are in Ottawa, and that they ought to receive the same consideration and increase. It is only the inside service at Ottawa whose salaries, increases, and classification are regulated by statute. In the vast majority of the other cases, those outside of Ottawa, the officials are either regulated by order in council or ministerial orders, and in most cases are paid out of large votes which are under the control of the minister and the department which utilizes these votes. These votes may be increased any time parliament chooses or whenever the minister brings down an estimate and parliament chooses to pass it. With regard to the inside service at Ottawa, a minister might bring down a vote and parliament might pass it, but if -the vote were not in accord with the provisions of the Civil Service Act, unless the individual officer is specially excepted by these magic words we used to have so often, and which I hope will not appear again in the government estimates, namely, ' Contrary to the Civil Service Act,' no salary could be increased except as provided by that Act. Since the first of September all the officers 31
who were in the outside service at Ottawa, and who previously were eligible for promotion or change or increase in salaries, according to the opinion of the minister, were put out of the vote given by parliament in a lump sum to pay those officers and for other purposes too very often. Those officers will now come under the Act subject to its restrictions and regulations, and their salaries can only be increased under a definite statutory provision.
Mv hon. friend is not aware-never having looked into the matter, I suppose, from that point of view-of the great amount of increases which have already been given the outside service in the way I have indicated. There have been large votes taken in parliament, increases of lump votes out of which those outside services were paid, which have amounted in some cases to hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the salaries of the outside services of the country have been increased from time to time fully as much, if not more,-in some instances decidedly more,

 than this Act is going to increase the salaries of the inside service at Ottawa. I have here a statement prepared by the Finance Department, in which I find that in the aggregate, in the last five years, the outside service have had increases given them on their salaries amounting to $1,409,000:
Marine and Fisheries Department	 $ 47,038
Inland Revenue	 5,350
Customs	 345,222
Northwest Mounted	Police ..	50,000
Indian Affairs	 9,300
Railways and Canals	 647,000
Printing Bureau	 50,500
These are the increases which have been voted at the request of ministers, in lump sums, out of which the salaries of these outside officials were paid.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that the total amount for a period of years, and, if so, what period?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is the total of the increases that have been given at different times during the last five years. These are increases which, when once given, go on every year. If they had been given five years ago, there would have been five times that amount paid out of the public chest to the outside service; but that is not the case. In some instances they have been given by general votes. For instance, I think that two years ago the Minister of Customs got a vote of $100,000 extra for his outside service, and some years ago the Post Office Department got a large sum to increase the pay of the outside service in that department, the aggregate of which amounted to about $250,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is the aggregate increase for the Customs Department?



r

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: $345,000 in the last five years. I think I am safe in saying that these are increases which were made at certain times, and they have been going on every year since.
Are these actual increases to officials, or do they apply to the natural increase in the outside service resulting from the increasing needs of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I asked that question and was told that they were increases to existing officials' salaries, and not increases to the number of offices or officers.
There are two ways of increasing salaries. For instance, postmasters got 40 per cent of the revenues of the office, and if the revenues of the office went up, their salaries went up correspondingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am informed that their salaries were increased apart from that. If there was an increase to 50 per cent, that would be included in these figures. Now, I take for granted that to, the Post Office Department and the Customs Department would apply my hon. friend's description of a public servant in the city of Ottawa doing work for the government on one side of the street, and another doing work for the government on the other side of the street, and one getting an increase and the other not. I have not details to show how much the clerks in the city of Ottawa Post Office have had their salaries increased during the last five years, but as the Postmaster General has been giving increases throughout the country, I have no doubt the city of Ottawa post office has had its share.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: Allow me to explain that the increase to which my hon. friend refers has not been applied to the clerks in the outside service, properly speaking That is covered by the increase which I obtained from parliament for postmasters some years ago. The House may remember that Sir Wm. Mulock, when Postmaster Genera], obtained an increase in the salaries of small postmasters from $12 to $25, and three years ago I obtained a further increase to $35. That acounts for most of that increase. The clerks who are under the statute receive their statutory increases, but there has been no special increase in the salaries of the outside service of the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
These figures indicate that a very great improvement has been made in the pay of the general outside service. There may be portions of the outside service which have not reaped the advantage, while there are other portions which have reaped a very great advantage The figures do not indicate how many there Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
are in each category; but they show that the government has not been unmindful of the needs and desires of the outside service. I want to point out that these increases were possible without an amendment to any particular statute, and are consequently in an entirely different position from the increases made to the inside (service, which are made by a definite statute. That is why in this particular case we have introduced a statute and asked parliament to pass it, while in the other case we do not require to do so, as an annual vote in the estimates of each dep-partment will accomplish the result desired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the Minister of Customs inform us whether the $345,000 included in the statement read by the Minister of Agriculture represents an actual annual increase to the outside officials of his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: On that point I cannot speak positively. When I take an extra vote, as I did this year, a certain amount <*f it we hope to use in increasing the salaries of the men in the service, and a certain amount we estimate may be required for new offices. Therefore, I cannot tell positively. I would have to inquire.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would be good enough to inquire. I know there have been substantial increases, but I do not think they amounted to so much as the sum mentioned in the statement of the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have here a copy of the Labour Gazette, which states that the increase of wages granted in 1907 to various employees of the Customs Department amounted to $160,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is quite possible that the person who compiled the figures for the Labour Gazette may have taken the whole $160,000 to represent increases, while a portion of that may have been utilized by the Customs Department for the payment of new officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am informed not.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: There was one year, two or three years ago, when we took an extra amount of $250,000. I remember we took a very large amount; so it is possible that is correct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Those amounts have been continued after once being taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: If they have been given to the same individual. If one died, for instance, and a new man came in, sometimes we started him at a little less.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
To show that what I said was correct, here is another item with regard to the Department of Indian Affairs.

It gives the actual number of employees; it says: 39 had their salaries increased by from $60 to $300 per annum and aggregating $9,360. That refers altogether to the outside service, it gives the number of the employees and the increase of their salaries.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is another point to which I would like to direct the attention of the hon. Minister of Agriculture and the Governor General. Section 8 of the Civil Service Act of last year reads as follows:
8. As soon as practicable after the coming into force of the Act, the head of each department should cause the organization of his department to be determined and defined by order in council, due regard being had to the status of each officer or clerk as the case may be.
2.	The order in council shall give the names of the several branches of the department, with the number and character of the offices, clerkships and other positions in each, and the duties, titles and salaries thereafter to pertain thereto.
3.	After being so determined and defined, the organization of a department should not be changed except by order in council.
It does not seem to me that that has been done by many 'of the departments; 'apparently it has been done to some extent by the Department of Inland Revenue; it may have been done by some other departments. It is a statutory provision, it is imperative in its language. It declares that the head of each department shall cause the organization of his department to be determined and defined by order in council, arid that the order in council shall set forth the duties appertaining to each office, clerkship and other position. The provisions of this statute seem to have been almost entirely disregarded in the various departments. I would not like to assert positively that ministers of the Crown who have disregarded it have been guilty of a criminal offence, although there is a law upon the statute-book that any person wilfully disobeying a statute is liable to indictment. Of course I have regard to the language of the statute, which is that this work of reorganization shall be done as soon as practicable after the coming into force of the Act. I am ready to concede that if a minister could show that he had devoted every available portion of his time to this work, and had not completed it, he might be able to escape criminal liability. But as it is, I think there would be a good case at least for calling him before a grand jury on a preliminary investigation. At all events, it is a matter that requires explanation. I consider it a very important part of the provisions of that section. You are to define, not only the salaries, not only the character of the offices, clerkships and other positions, but what is absolutely im-311
portant to a thorough organization of the department, you are to make known by the terms of an order in council the duties which each clerk is called upon to perform as a public servant of Canada. That has not been done; there has heen little pretense of doing it. I would again invite the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture to that, and ask him to explain why the provisions of the statute in that regard have not been complied with.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I have just 'phoned the accountant of the Customs Department in reference to that matter. He tells me that it was he who gave those figures, and that those are the actual increases granted to the men who were in the service, and do not include new offices.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I remember well the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition which he made with regard to this matter before, and I have looked up a little the orders in council. Perhaps the orders in council might be more full than they are. I have just sent for a copy of the order in council in my own department, and I would like my hon. friend to follow me a little, and I will show him what we have done, which I think is fairly fulfilling the intention of the Act, though I grant that we might go a little further in an elaborate description of the work of a good many offices. Beginning with the first division of subdivision A:	Dr. Montizambert,
Director General of Public Health. I do not know that I could define much more particularly what the duties of Dr. Monti-zamhert are. I might go on to say that he is in charge of the quarantine service of Canada, and give 'other /particulars ,and practically transcribe the order in council appointing him, but I do not think that is intended or desired.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would say that where the order in council appointing an officer has prescribed his duties fairly well, the statute would be sufficiently complied with if reference were made to that order in council; in other words, the duties of this officer shall be those set forth in the order in council appointing him on such a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Then I pass over Dr. Saunders, Mr. Blue, Dr. Rutherford and so on. We come down to the first division of subdivision B. Dr. James Fletcher, Entomologist and Botanist, Central Experimental Farm; Mr. Shutt, chemist of experimental farm; Mr. St. Denis, secretary of the Census and Statistics office. I should think that was a fairly fair description of the duties of the offices which these gentlemen hold. J. H. Grisdale, agriculturist, Central Experimental Farm. As a matter of fact, in the Treasury Board the descrip-cions of the officers at the experimental farm are just the same as they are put in

the order in council. Dr. Charles Saunders, cerealist. Perhaps that requires some explanation to most people, but it defines the office of the individual. When you come down further to the lower subdivisions, as a general rule, they are simply clerks, sometimes perhaps doing one thing, and sometimes another. I do not think in most of the lower orders of the service we can do much more than define them as clerks, unless they have some particular work. I have here Mr. C. Martin, assistant editor of the Archives. He is the gentleman who helps to edit the bulletins and publications that go out from the Archives. D. Drummond, live stock inspector; Mr. McKae, live stock inspector; Mr. McMurray, French correspondent, experimental farm. Then here is Mr. Watson, stenographer; Mr. Nolan, patent examiner. I hardly think it could be expected that we should go much beyond that. I confess I did think in so doing that I would be free from any likelihood of prosecution under the Criminal Code for dereliction of duty. But would it be well to encumber the orders in council with more graphic descriptions of the work done?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In some departments the reply is that there is nothing whatever. For example, in the Department of Justice there is no information available of the nature asked for in this address. The Auditor General reports the same thing; other departments report the same thing. The Minister of Inland Revenue seems to have complied with the statute and to have done his work in this connection far better than any other minister, with the exception possibly of the Minister of Agriculture, whose records I have not examined very closely. He has absolutely defined the duties of the heads of each branch and has given a fair indication of the duties of the various officers in the branch. For example, take his organization of the Department of Inland Revenue:
Deputy Minister-The duties of the Deputy
Minister of Inland Revenue shall cover the general supervision and administration of all branches of the Inland Revenue Department.
Then he names his clerks, stenographers and typewriters.
Secretary-The duties of this officer shall be to attend to all correspondence, other than of an administrative character, have charge of all records and supplies, and to have general supervision over the correspondence and supply branches.
Then he goes on to deal with the various officers of the secretary's branch. Dealing with the chief accountant he says:
The duties of this officer shall be to have general control and supervision over all work connected with revenue and expenditure, the work of the statistical branches of all services and the preparation of the financial and statistical reports.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Then he goes on to deal with subdivision A of. the first division and proceeds:
The number and character of the officers in the Accountant's branch to be as follows:
1. Assistant accountant-To have particular charge of accounts relative to receipts and expenditure, to record each deposit of revenue, to have charge of the general journal and ledger and to replace the chief accountant when absent from any cause.
And so on with reference to every important office of his department. Then he has taken up the laboratory branch and dealt with it in the same way very thoroughly. 1 understand from my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), although I have not seen the organization of the Mines Department, that this has been done equally well. The other departments should have devoted the same attention to the statute and observed the same particularity and definiteness in prescribing the duties of the various officers that we find in the organization carried out by the Minister of Inland Revenue and Mines. Otherwise, a great part of the advantage from this statute will be lost.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I perfectly agree with my hon. friend that so far as it is possible and consistent with conciseness the intention of the Act was to indicate these things in the classification. I think it probable that when another classification is issued that will he done to a greater extent.

I do not want to prolong the discussion but there were two points that might be considered as being assented to, made by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, if they were not noted. In the first place he seemed to argue that if the minister had a lump vote he could make any addition to the salaries of officers out of that lump vote that he chose.
I am not sure but that he has the absolute power to do it, but I do not think he has the right. For instance, he comes down with a lump vote, presents it to parliament and says this is to pay officers' salaries. How many officers have you?-so many. What salaries are they getting?- so much. It goes down in ' Hansard '. It is discussed here and parliament says: Yes, that vote is all right, because we know those officers are in the service, we know what they are getting and we think it is not unreasonable. I doubt very much if the minister has the right, after having made that compact with parliament, to go out and, three months afterwards, raise those salaries to any amount he chooses.
I do not think parliament will cavil at a reasonable addition if cause is shown but I should not like to let the theory go unchallenged that a minister has the right after having made the compact with parliament which he did, to add, out of that

lump vote, to the salaries of his officers whatever he chose. The other point is in regard to the elasticity of the Act. This new Act is elastic in this respect that specialists under it can be appointed and may be promoted. I am not at all sure but that my hon. friend would have kept better within the spirit of the Act if he had allowed Mr. Saunders to come in at the salary which he did and then taken the means at his disposal under the Act. If the requirements were reasonable parliament would have assented. I myself, after his presentation of the facts, would have raised no objection to the salary being increased. That could have been done under the Act because we must have the provisions sufficiently elastic as to allow such singular and notable case to be provided for.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They are provided for, no doubt. In my organization I was going to put certain officers in a certain classification, which, in my judgment, those officers ought to occupy and I did raise all those salaries to the minimum of the class in which they would come in the exercise of the power which I had. I think my hon. friend is putting an extreme case when he says that a minister, having made a compact with parliament, should not violate it. I quite agree with him but in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred there has been no such compact. A lump vote, it is understood, is going to pay for the service. Part of the payment for the service must be salaries. The distribution of the amount in salaries has never come before parliament and there has been no compact.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Excuse me, there has been no compact of any kind. The minister is obliged to keep within the vote but judgment is left to him as to how he shall spend that vote. He gives the usual explanations and if he went contrary to any of these explanations he would break the compact. There are a number of instances in which the salary of an individual is asked for and voted and under these circumstances it would not be fair to make a change in that person's salary. I do not think it would be consistent with the rights of parliament. But, in a general way, the details of these salaries never have been passed by parliament.

I beg my hon. friend's pardon. We have the Auditor General and the Auditor General puts upon the pages of his book which comes before us the name of every officer who receives a salary, and when we are going over the estimates, my hon. friend knows that the Auditor General's Report and the estimates go side by side and that we criticise the estimate with the Auditor General's Report in our hands. If we find any officer whom
we think is getting too much we make a protest. I am not going to say it is an actually signed contract, but it is an implied compact. One more point; I have drawn it to the attention of my hon. friend and the other ministers. Is it businesslike to take a lump sum of $200,000, $300,000 or $400,000, covering a dozen different things, and put that through without any itemizing at all, a portion of it for salaries, a portion of it for other things and nodivision at all as to that amount which is properly referable to salaries or as to the amount which it is properly referable to other operations and other things? In my time we had some lump votes, but I would' like my hon. friend to take an estimate of 1890, or from that up, and compare it with the estimate now and he will find that the tendency has been to give lump votes. The whole trouble in connection with the North Atlantic Trading Company business that we discussed so much arose from the fact that it was covered up in a lump vote and that the actual contract was entered into under a lump vote that covered a very large contract as my hon. friend will admit. If the vote had been divided as it ought to have been that could not have happened in the first instance. I do hope, although it may be too much to hope for, that succeeding estimates will show more sub-division so that we can define things a little more accurately. The ministers ought not have too much power. It is a great temptation. If your back bencher comes to you and wants something and you can show him you have a special vote for that and your vote will not allow it you have an answer, but if he shows you a vote of $400,000 out of which you can take whatever you like for any purpose, you are shorn of an argument that I am sure the Minister of Agriculture must often want to have.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I can asure my hon. friend I am glad to have that answer whenever I can get it. In bringing the outside service in Ottawa under the civil government we have taken a long step in the direction of what my hon. friend (Mr. Foster! has said.
That is one of the best features of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think it is quite likely we will take other steps in the course of time.

His rise has been very rapid. What are the reasons for it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The reason assigned is that jhe was competent and deserving, in the estimation of the heads of the department.

In that department there are many clerks who were in the service long before 1900 and who have presumably performed their duties well. It would seem that other things being equal the official of longer service should get the promotion. This clerk's rise was very rapid; the salary increased from $400 to $1,600 in eight years and he is now put at the minimum of a class that allows him still further range at the rate of $100 a year. Is the minister very sure there were no other older employees who might have had claims to that

promotion? On what principle was this man jumped over the others?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only answer that it is possible to give is that his work has been found satisfactory and he has been given work of a character that when properly performed entitled him to this increase of remuneration. My hon. friend, of course, knows that it is impossble to absolutely give every man in a large department the same opportunity of showing the good^ there is in him; the work of one section is not as important as that of another, and the man whose fortune it is to be in the section of less important work, even although he may be a good man, has not the same opportunity to show his ability as the man who, by fortune, has been placed in the section of the department requiring a higher class of work. I presume that this man was fortunate in being placed in the section of the department requiring the greater ability and that he showed the ability and received the remuneration.

I concede that the position of a minister is sometimes difficult; he wants to advance a deserving clerk and at the same time he wants to avoid any injustice to equally deserving clerks in his employ. It would seem, however, that the minister should be able to ascertain the relative capacity of the clerks even in different sections of his department. It is not good for the morale of the department that there should be any sense of injustice among the employees; they want to see a fair deal, and if one clerk is advanced very rapidly, others may feel that they are being treated unjustly. I presume that the minister is pretty sure that he has not done an injustice to any older clerks in that department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In this particular case, I am informed that this gentleman is senior in his class, that is to say he is not being advanced over any one in his class.
All I can do is to call the minister's attention' to it, he is the boss after all.
I see an item providing a salary for a timber inspector. What are the arrangements in regard to timber inspection that you engage an inspector by the year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A great deal of the value of the Indian property in the northern part of the province is in the timber on their lands and in order te get the best results for the Indians, it is necessary that we should employ some one responsible to the department who has a knowledge of timber to make the necessary inspection. Mr. Chitty is the gentleman who discharges that duty.
The department has sufficient work, I suppose, to keep him practically busy all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amount of timber held by the Indians in the northern part of the province is very large and there is ample work for him to do.
Will my hon. friend explain the two remaining clerks to be promoted ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. O'Connor was appointed February 15, 1898. He was promoted to a second class clerkship July 1, 1905. He is employed in the Lands and Timber branch and came in at $400.

is all ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The work in his branch of timber and lands has greatly increased during the past two or three years owing to the amount of Indian lands which have been ^rendered and sold, and in that increase of work this gentleman has borne his part very creditably, and we felt warranted in promoting him from time to time.
How many in his branch?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: ' Eight.
Has he superseded any who are older than himself ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In that branch there are a number of ladies, and we have not given them that promotion to the higher branches which possibly the merits of their actual work would warrant, because it is not considered that, in the nature of things, they are able to take the higher positions for which we have to train men and promote them. But aside from that point, Mr. O'Connor has the seniority in that branch.
How many ladies in ttiat branch ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Four.

I am sorry _ to hear the opinion expressed by the minister that, in these days of equality, equal merit in a lady does not entitle her to equal payment with a man. He will have to fight that out with the four ladies in that department and may have a pretty _ hard time. Will the hon. gentleman explain the next one ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Ogilvie entered in 1904 as temporary clerk; he was made permanent second-class on August 25, 1905. He got on entering $1,000. He is an architect and does drafting and arranging for the buildings for the department. He is a trained architect.
And Mr. Chitty ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He came in at $1,000 in 1893. His salary was increased to $1,200 on July 1, 1898 and to $1,500 on July 1, 1905, He is a timber inspector.

No other new clerks except the law clerk and promotions?

speechtext: No.
I would like an explanation with regard to the twenty brought in. Were they in the employment outside and for what period ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They were all old employees.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

It is usual to have provision for additional help, if it is required. Under the former Civil Service Act there was provision made for taking on extra clerks. Now we think it is desirable to have at least $1,000 available for that purpose.
